title: FSSAI Cracks Down on Misleading Food Claims, Forces Bournvita Maker to Withdraw Health Labels
excerpt: India's food regulator has issued over 150 notices to major brands including Nestlé, PepsiCo, and Coca-Cola, banning '100%' claims and unsubstantiated health promises from packaging.
body:
• Mondelez India, the maker of Bournvita, has withdrawn health and nutrient-comparison claims from its packaging and removed related advertisements from e-commerce platforms after FSSAI enforcement action.
  • FSSAI has issued more than 150 notices to food companies including Nestlé India, PepsiCo, Coca-Cola India, Abbott India, Red Bull India, Danone India, and Ferrero India over misleading claims.
  • The regulator's May 2025 advisory banning the use of "100%" on food labels is now being enforced, with Amway India removing the term from its coconut oil packaging.
  • Enforcement has expanded to 12 e-commerce companies and over 30 food-service establishments, including major restaurant chains.

India's food safety regulator is forcing some of the world's largest food companies to strip misleading claims from their products. Mondelez India Foods, which makes Bournvita and Cadbury products, has withdrawn health and nutrient-comparison claims flagged by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and removed related advertisements from e-commerce platforms, according to The Hindu.

Over 150 Notices to Major Brands

The Bournvita action is part of a broader enforcement sweep. FSSAI has issued more than 150 notices to food companies over misleading advertisements, false claims, and labelling violations. The list includes Nestlé India, PepsiCo, Coca-Cola India, Abbott India, Red Bull India, Danone India, Monster Energy India, Ferrero India, and Kenvue.

Bournvita first came under scrutiny in 2023 when social media influencer Revant Himatsingka — known as Food Pharmer — questioned the drink's sugar content and its marketing as a health beverage for children. Mondelez served Himatsingka a legal notice, and he took down the video. But the controversy triggered a wider regulatory examination of how packaged food brands market their products in India.

The End of '100% Pure' Claims

In May 2025, FSSAI issued an advisory asking all food businesses to stop using the term "100%" on labels, packaging, and promotional content. The regulator said the term is not defined under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, or its advertising regulations — and could create "a false impression of absolute purity or superiority."

"The use of the term '100%' — whether in isolation or combined with other descriptors — is likely to create a false impression of absolute purity or superiority. This could mislead consumers into believing that other comparable products in the market are inferior."

— FSSAI spokesperson

That advisory is now producing results. Amway India has removed "100%" from its "100% Pure Coconut Oil" packaging and dropped the "Energy Drink" label from its caffeinated XS range. Kerala-based Juza Foods has agreed to withdraw claims such as "boost immunity," "support stronger bones," and comparative calcium claims from its baby-food products.

E-Commerce and Restaurants in the Crosshairs

FSSAI's enforcement has expanded beyond product packaging. The regulator has issued 12 notices to e-commerce companies selling food products with unverified claims, and more than 30 notices to food-service establishments, including major restaurant chains. Under the Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018, all claims must be truthful, unambiguous, and backed by evidence.

The monitoring committee set up by FSSAI to scrutinize food advertisements across social media, e-commerce, and traditional platforms has reported 138 cases of non-compliance in a recent six-month period alone, targeting leading brands for misleading claims.

A Shifting Landscape for Indian Consumers

The enforcement wave signals a change in how India regulates food marketing. For decades, packaged food brands operated with minimal scrutiny over health claims. The 2023 Bournvita controversy, driven by social media pressure, became a turning point — pushing FSSAI into action on claims that had gone unchallenged for years.

Whether the current enforcement sustains its momentum or faces pushback from an industry that generates over $100 billion in annual revenue remains to be seen. But for Indian consumers navigating aisles of products labelled "100% natural" or "immunity boosting," the regulator is now asking brands to prove what they print — or take it off the shelf.
